strengths: Novel and practically motivated application: applying discrete graph denoising diffusion to ad hoc directional-antenna network topology generation, with an operational correction algorithm.
The CAM-token idea is plausible and reasonably integrated into a graph transformer/diffusion framework to provide graph-level conditioning beyond local message passing.
The paper reports constraint-oriented metrics (connectedness, isolated/saturated nodes, parity, length) and an ablation suggesting the added loss terms improve parity and antenna-sector saturation.
The partial-diffusion network-evolution idea is conceptually simple and attractive for maintaining topologies under node movement.
weaknesses: Central claims are not adequately supported: generated graphs deviate substantially from target/dataset topologies (Table 2: 49.74 vs 43.90 links, 16.19% vs 9.74% saturated antennas, 1.60 vs 1.72 throughput), so 'similar structural properties' and 'only minor corrections' are not convincingly demonstrated. No post-correction metrics are reported.

The network-evolution/partial-diffusion contribution is described but never experimentally evaluated; there are no moving-node experiments, stability measures, reconfiguration-quality comparisons, or overhead/latency results.

Reproducibility is insufficient: Algorithm 1 is high-level and omits the heuristic, interference threshold, antenna/sector model, parity construction, and dataset generation details; no code or data are provided, and architecture/training hyperparameters (layers, heads, dimensions, seeds, learning-rate schedule) are largely unspecified.

Evaluation is limited: only 16-node graphs are benchmarked; the 32-node claim is anecdotal ('seemed to display results similar'), there are no error bars or significance tests over runs, and no comparison to traditional greedy/exact topology optimization or other graph generative models.

The CAM-token contribution is not cleanly isolated: Table 1 compares NetDiff to 'NetDiff (no features)' and 'Standard GT', but does not separate CAM from features/losses. The claimed global-modulation benefit therefore remains unproven.

Several technical formulations are unclear or incorrect: Eq. 4 writes cross-attention without softmax; Eqs. 6-8 leave modulation dimensions/broadcasting ambiguous; Eq. 11's cosine-loss description and Eq. 12's parity loss do not clearly supervise true node parity; the angle formula contains an apparent typo. This undermines both soundness and reproducibility.

The throughput/interference simulation is not described, so the reported 'user throughput' numbers cannot be interpreted or reproduced; similarly, the operational correction algorithm's effect on final constraint violation and throughput is not measured.
Presentation quality is substandard for ICML: numerous typos, inconsistent notation, incomplete equations, and no dedicated limitations or failure-mode discussion.

Significance is hard to establish: the method is specialized to a synthetic small-scale setting, and it is not shown to outperform or complement combinatorial optimization on realistic network sizes or conditions.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely interesting and practically motivated problem: generating ad hoc network link topologies (with directional antennas) using deep graph generation, which is a comparatively underexplored application domain for DDPMs.

The system design is a reasonable integration of established components — discrete denoising diffusion (DiGress-style), edge-conditioned graph transformer, FiLM/register-style conditioning — augmented with CAM tokens, sector/angle/parity features, and corresponding constraint losses.

The partial-diffusion network-evolution idea (Sec. 4.3) is a sensible and non-trivial extension for maintaining topology stability under node mobility, with a meaningful motivation (avoiding full reconfiguration overhead).

Reported constraint adherence is high for several metrics (connectedness 99.13%, parity 98.65%, length 98.97%), and a post-processing/repair algorithm (Alg. 2) is provided to bridge generation and operability.
weaknesses: Central claims are undermined by internally inconsistent results. Table 3 reports that a standard BCE model achieves only 67.07% parity, yet Table 1 reports the 'Standard GT' (presumably the same ablative baseline) at 98.59% parity. The text asserts the parity loss term is 'mandatory,' but Table 1 shows a model without the relevant features/losses already at ~98.6%. This contradiction is not explained and directly weakens the paper's main evidence that the added losses are necessary.

No ablation isolates the primary architectural novelty (CAM tokens). Table 1 contrasts 'NetDiff' (features + CAM) with 'NetDiff (no features)' and 'Standard GT,' so the individual contribution of CAM is never measured against a features-only baseline. The claim that CAM improves 'global control' rests on a single saturated-nodes number (12.31% vs 17.08%).

Evaluation lacks any comparison to competing methods. Despite building directly on DiGress, no comparison is made to it or to other graph-generation baselines; the only baselines are ablations of the authors' own model. Crucially, there is no quality or runtime comparison against the greedy algorithm (Alg. 1) that the paper explicitly aims to replace, so the claimed efficiency advantage (O(n^2) vs O(m^2)) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is poor. The dataset is not described (size, node distribution, how many graphs, train/val/test split), and the labeling algorithm (Alg. 1) is deliberately left vague ('without entering into technical details'). No code release, no full hyperparameters, and no error bars / variance over runs are reported. Others could not reliably reproduce or build on this.

Several equations are garbled or inconsistent, indicating insufficient care: the edge-angle definition uses identical indices throughout (arctan of 0/0), and sector-loss notation alternates between n_i^s and n_s^i. The cosine loss (Eq. 11) is ambiguously specified.

Key operational figures are unsupported by methodology. The 'user throughput' column in Table 2 has no described simulation or estimation procedure, yet it is used to argue the generated graphs approach the target performance.

Strong real-world claims ('require only minor corrections and verification steps to be operational') are not validated in any network simulation or testbed; they rest on a heuristic post-processing algorithm whose own correctness ('it almost never disconnects the graph') is asserted without measurement.

Limited evidential scope: benchmarks are on 16-node sets, and the 32-node results are only qualitative ('seemed to display results similar') due to an inability to generate a full dataset — a gap the paper acknowledges but does not resolve.

strengths: Targets an interesting and under-explored application: generating ad hoc directional-antenna network topologies with a conditional graph diffusion model.

Combines discrete denoising diffusion with a graph transformer and introduces Cross-Attentive Modulation (CAM) tokens to inject global graph-level conditioning; this is a reasonable architectural idea that could be useful beyond this application.

Adds problem-specific node/edge features and auxiliary losses (sector occupancy, cosine, parity) that appear to improve constraint adherence in the reported ablations (e.g., parity 98.65% vs 67.07% with standard BCE).
Proposes a partial-diffusion procedure for network evolution under node movement, which is conceptually sensible for maintaining stable topology over time.
Includes a post-processing correction algorithm to handle redundant links and disconnected components, showing awareness of operational deployment needs.
weaknesses: Central claims about realism, operational readiness, and temporal stability are not adequately supported by experiments. The paper reports only static 16-node benchmarks and qualitative claims that 32 nodes give similar results, but no actual 32-node results; the network-evolution/partial-diffusion component is described without any empirical evaluation.

Evaluation is narrow. The main baseline is a standard graph transformer; there is no comparison to the greedy algorithm used to generate the dataset, to combinatorial/heuristic baselines, or to other modern graph generative models (e.g., DiGress, MIDI), making it unclear whether the learned approach outperforms or even matches non-neural approaches in solution quality or runtime.

Important architectural ablation is missing: CAM tokens are a main claimed contribution, but the reported comparisons (NetDiff vs. NetDiff no features vs. standard GT) do not clearly isolate the effect of CAM versus handcrafted features/losses. Table 3 only examines loss effects, not CAM.

Reproducibility is insufficient: dataset construction, training set size, number of graphs, exact model dimensions, optimizer schedule, noise schedule parameters, and evaluation simulation details are missing; no code or data are provided. Several equations also contain apparent typos (e.g., the edge-angle formula in Section 4.2).

Operational claims are overstated. The model still needs a correction algorithm (up to 250 ms), generates substantially more saturated antennas (16.19% vs. target 9.74%) and more links than target (49.74 vs. 43.90), and simulated throughput is below target (1.60 vs. 1.72), so 'minor corrections' and 'operational' are not convincingly demonstrated.

The method is evaluated on constraints and simple graph properties but not on end-to-end network performance metrics such as interference, scheduling, packet delay, or throughput under realistic physical models. This weakens the significance for wireless networking.

Presentation quality is uneven: some notation is undefined or ambiguous (e.g., parity target construction, odd-pair link constraint, transition matrix m), and the connection to some cited works and formal problem setting could be clearer.

strengths: Addresses a practical and challenging problem: joint link-topology and transmit/receive parity generation for directional mobile ad hoc networks under global constraints.
Proposes ACAM tokens, an interesting absolute cross-attention mechanism without softmax that can aggregate/count global graph properties in a permutation-invariant and O(n) way.
Introduces partial diffusion for fast topology updates under mobility, with some evidence that few denoising steps can reuse previous topologies while satisfying constraints.
Includes ablations for the additional loss terms (Table 4), showing that domain-specific losses substantially improve parity and saturation.
The impact statement is thoughtful and acknowledges risks of misuse and over-reliance on generated topologies.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is severely limited: no code or dataset is provided, and key simulation parameters such as antenna radiation patterns, propagation models, and attenuation laws are explicitly omitted as proprietary, making the central results impossible to verify or build upon.
The evaluation lacks comparison to the most directly relevant recent method, TopoFormer, which addresses a closely related topology-generation problem, despite being cited in related work.

Main quantitative comparisons in Table 2 report throughput without uncertainty estimates or statistical significance, and the improvement over the strong DDPM-GT baseline is small (e.g., 75.43 to 78.92 Mbps at 16 nodes), so robustness of the gains is unclear.

The ACAM ablation is incomplete: there is no comparison against other global-information mechanisms such as virtual nodes or explicit statistical features, and no direct analysis of whether the unsoftmaxed aggregation actually induces counting or improves permutation-invariant global coherence beyond the reported saturation changes.

Partial diffusion is evaluated only against the paper's own general framework; there is no comparison to recomputing from scratch, other update strategies, or the reference solver, and claims such as '21% more similar' and '3.3 to 5 times faster computation' are not defined precisely or supported with wall-clock timings.

The claim of 'constant inference time' is misleading: while ACAM tokens are O(n), graph-transformer edge attention scales quadratically with the number of nodes, and no runtime comparison across graph sizes is reported.

Presentation has several technical and typographical issues: the edge-angle equation contains an apparent error (e_i^2 - e_i^2), notation is inconsistent (e.g., S versus \widehat{S}), and there are unclear passages such as 'using without any post-processing' and missing details on trajectory generation and reconfiguration thresholds.

The dataset construction mixes quasi-exhaustive search with a heuristic fallback, but the proportion, quality, and potential label noise of the fallback solutions are not analyzed, and the target is itself the output of that solver rather than an independently verified optimum.
Several constraint-satisfaction improvements over the DDPM-GT baseline are marginal (e.g., parity 98.59 vs. 98.64), yet the paper draws strong conclusions about global capability improvements.

Key experimental details are missing: the number of test graphs, variance across graphs, full training dataset size for the main model, and exact hyperparameters/architecture dimensions beyond a few high-level values.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: real-time topology generation for directional mobile ad hoc networks with half-duplex/parity, sector, interference, and connectivity constraints.

Introduces domain-specific edge/node features and auxiliary losses (sector occupancy, cosine angle, parity) that are sensible ways to inject hard structural constraints into a diffusion training objective.

ACAM tokens are a computationally efficient, permutation-invariant mechanism for injecting global graph-level information via unsoftmaxed cross-attention and FiLM modulation; the ablation suggests some benefit over CAM and DDPM-GT.
Partial diffusion for topology updates under mobility is a natural and practically relevant extension, with reported speedups and continuity improvements over full diffusion.
The manuscript is generally structured, with implementation details such as diffusion steps, model dimensions, optimizer settings, and architecture blocks.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is severely limited: the training data come from a proprietary simulation and quasi-exhaustive solver, key antenna/propagation parameters are omitted, and no code or dataset is provided. This prevents independent verification and makes the reported numbers difficult to build upon.

The evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous: experiments focus on 16-node graphs (32-node results in the appendix), the number of test graphs is not stated, throughput results lack variance or statistical significance, and baselines are weak/untuned.

No comparison is made to combinatorial or optimization-based solvers on small instances, nor to the closely related TopoFormer method, despite it being cited as solving a similar problem. The 'Target' labels themselves may be suboptimal because the reference solver relies on a heuristic fallback.

Central claims are only partially supported. The improvement over DDPM-GT is modest (e.g., saturation 12.1 vs 13.6; throughput 78.92 vs 75.43 for 16 nodes), and the 'over 95% of target' claim is questionable for 32 nodes (about 94.7%). The 'constant inference time' claim is unclear given variable partial-diffusion steps.

The ACAM novelty is incremental and not rigorously justified. Unsoftmaxed cross-attention is closely related to linear attention, virtual nodes, and attention registers; there is no theoretical analysis of the claimed 'counting' behavior and no ablation isolating softmax removal from token count or FiLM modulation.

Partial diffusion is essentially partial noising/inpainting of a previous graph, but the paper does not compare against existing partial-diffusion or graph-editing methods, nor does it provide detailed accuracy-vs-speed tradeoff curves. The reported continuity metric is not clearly defined.

Presentation has multiple clarity issues: several equations (sector loss, cosine loss, parity loss) contain notation errors or ambiguities, the use of post-processing is inconsistent with the claim that results exclude post-processing, and some references contain year/duplicate errors.

There is no real-world deployment validation, hardware/embedded latency measurement, failure-case analysis, or scaling study beyond 32 nodes. The impact statement is generic and the limitations of the method are not adequately discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and constrained real-world problem: jointly generating directional communication links and transmit/receive parity for mobile ad hoc networks under sector, interference, connectivity, and half-duplex constraints.

The discrete node-conditioned diffusion formulation is sensible for this task and avoids a post-hoc parity assignment, which is a meaningful modelling choice given the coupling between parity and feasible links.

The proposed ACAM tokens are an interesting architectural idea: detaching global tokens from message passing and using unsoftmaxed cross-attention with FiLM modulation is a plausible way to inject graph-level cardinality information in a permutation-invariant way.

Partial diffusion for network reconfiguration is a useful contribution for temporal/mobile settings; the reported 10–15 step updates and 3.3–5× speedups are promising and the continuity results support the motivation.

The empirical study includes useful ablations: domain features, CAM vs. ACAM tokens, and the proposed loss terms are separately evaluated, showing consistent improvements over the DDPM-GT baseline and heuristic/omnidirectional baselines.
The paper does engage with ethical/impact considerations, acknowledging potential misuse and deployment risks.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited: the training data generation depends on proprietary antenna radiation patterns, propagation models, and simulation parameters that are explicitly omitted, and neither code nor the reference solver is released. This makes it difficult to replicate the dataset, target topologies, or throughput numbers.

The paper cites TopoFormer as a closely related method for the same topology-generation problem but does not empirically compare against it. Even if TopoFormer lacks joint parity prediction, a topology-only comparison or a parity-assignment variant would substantially strengthen the evaluation.

The main results focus on 16-node networks; 32-node results appear only in the appendix after retraining on a reduced mixed-size dataset for only about 2 epochs. The claim of size flexibility and 'constant inference time' is therefore not well supported, especially since attention and edge updates scale with graph size.

There is an unclear and potentially contradictory statement about post-processing: the text says results exclude post-processing, but later describes a correction routine to enforce hard constraints and restore connectivity. It is not clear which reported constraint-satisfaction metrics are raw model outputs and which are corrected.

The theoretical motivation for ACAM's 'counting' ability is not rigorously analyzed or directly tested; the experiments compare CAM vs. ACAM only through aggregate saturation/throughput metrics, and no comparison to standard virtual nodes or softmaxed cross-attention is given.

The target labels are produced by a quasi-exhaustive solver with a heuristic fallback, but the fraction of fallback cases and the optimality gap of the supervision are not quantified. This matters because the model is trained to imitate targets that may themselves be suboptimal.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: the edge-angle formula appears garbled, variables such as s and epsilon in the noise schedule are not clearly defined, and there are typos such as 'noise-less reconfiguration framework'.

The experimental setup relies on a single random seed (123) and many throughput/constraint metrics lack error bars or significance tests, making it hard to judge the robustness of small reported improvements.
The paper has no dedicated limitations section and does not discuss failure modes, scaling to realistic network sizes, or sensitivity to solver quality beyond the appendix.

The claimed 'over 95% of target performance' is not uniformly supported: for 32-node throughput, the reported value is about 94.7% of target, and the target itself is a solver-generated reference rather than a true optimum.
